Saung Gauk屬弦鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs編號322.11: The saung gauk is a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 322.11. Its arched-harp tradition may have reached Burma from Mesopotamia by way of India; a relief at the Bawbawgyi stupa of the Sri Ksetra dynasty, from around the middle of the sixth century, already shows an arched harp of about five strings, and Chinese records of the same period note Pyu musicians playing it. The Ava dynasty produced the eleven-string inward-curving arch; in the Konbaung dynasty Siamese court musicians brought a new form, and Myawaddy Mingyi U Sa raised the count to thirteen strings and established the Yodaya type. It reached the Qing court in the eighteenth century and was played as tribute from 1788.

The right hand plucks from the outside, and the left hand stops the strings to make the notes clear and give them a detached attack; when a note has to be damped, the nail of the left thumb presses the string from the inside to raise its tension. Tuning was traditionally done by twisting the string bindings, and new instruments may use tuning pegs. Playing is usually with a singer, who keeps the tempo with a bell and clappers while the harp follows the voice. A learner can first get the order of holding, plucking, left-hand damping and tuning, then practise the traditional tuning and fingering.

The top of the body is covered with deer skin and lacquered red, with four round soundholes; the neck is carved from a tree root, and the source says a curved root of the sha tree improves the tension. The strings are silk or nylon, finished with red cotton tassels. The body and the stand are decorated with mica, glass, gilding and red and black lacquer, and the end of the neck carries a bodhi-leaf ornament. The source does not state the wood of the body itself.

Before the nineteenth century it was played mainly in court chamber music, and afterwards it also entered more intimate chamber settings. It is often paired with a singer, who keeps the tempo with a bell and clappers while the harp follows the voice. Burmese classical music has different modes, and players also developed the Mandalay technique. It also appears at Qing-dynasty Chinese court banquets and is associated with Burmese classical traditions such as the Yodaya.

The treble is bright and crisp, with a jewelled, pleasing ring; the middle register is warm and full and highly expressive; the bass is steady and deep, with plenty of resonance. Its range is wide, spanning more than three octaves. The harp uses horsehair strings and a wooden resonating box, and the vibrating strings resonate with the box to give a warm, distinctively national resonance. Compared with the Western harp, the saung gauk is gentler and more restrained, with an Eastern character; it is close to the Thai harp, also a Southeast Asian instrument, but sounds deeper. Its sound has many layers, and it can carry a delicate, elegant solo as well as weave with other instruments into a warm, harmonious atmosphere.

The saung gauk (Saung Gauk) is the arched horizontal harp of traditional Burmese music and is also regarded as the national instrument. It is a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 322.11. The body is a horizontal resonating box whose top is covered with deer skin and pierced by four round soundholes, and the long, curved neck is carved from a tree root; thirteen to sixteen silk or nylon strings run diagonally from the string bar to the neck. The player sits on the floor with the body on the lap and the neck to the left, plucking with the right hand and stopping the strings with the left. It was once used in court chamber music, later also in intimate chamber settings, and it often accompanies a singer.
